pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

schema.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

entries.description: Get information on a specific pull request in GitHub repository.

after.description: Cursor for pagination, used only by the get_review_comments method. Pass the endCursor from the previous page's PageInfo to fetch the next page.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)

{"number":874,"title":"PlanNG: static site header; trip links and export buttons removed","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ue?thread=cmsg_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ueByrxpEUJLEwyf2X7F85uBb)_

Before: choosing a festival on the timeline rewrote the top bar: the festival's wordmark, its city as the third nav link, a city-and-dates hint, and its accent colour. Under the calendar sat a "While you're here" row of partner links (bed, airport transfer, trains) and two export buttons (itinerary CSV, calendar ICS) with a note.

After: the top bar is the same on every festival. It shows **EdFringeNow** and **Now · Plan · Festivals** in the house palette, with no hint. The trip links, the export buttons and their note are gone from the page. The footer's partner-link disclosure goes too, since there are no partner links left to disclose.

The trip-link builder (`site/planNG/festivals.js`) and the export module (`site/plan/lib/itinerary.js`) stay, so both features can be placed somewhere else later.

How:
- **Header:** the wordmark is static markup. `renderChrome()` names the third link with `nav.festivals`. The hint and its `header.run` string are removed. `.site-header` pins the colour tokens to the house palette on an opaque background.
- **Calendar card:** the trip-links and plan-actions markup is removed, along with `renderTripLinks`, `renderOriginLine`, `wireExports`, their CSS and their now-unused strings. The four trip labels stay as `unrendered` strings for the builder.

Spec:
- `18.1` and `23.6` are rewritten for the static header. `18.1`'s golden stacks the header on two festivals to show they match.
- `18.6`, `18.7` and `24.2` move from behavior to logic leaves, proved against the builder rather than the page.
- New `24.5` carries the asked-once half of the old `24.2`.
- `24.3` no longer asserts trip links.
- The goldens that move with the header or the shorter page are refreshed.

Checks: `npm test` 355/355, `npm run test:ui` 147/147, `npm run verify` clean.

{"number":875,"title":"PlanNG: set the trip's dates on the year strip, with flights either side","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ue?thread=cmsg_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ueSy7tJ2c4nKE9muVjPheAyd)_

Before: clicking a festival on the year strip decided everything. It set the planning period to that festival's run, the theme and the URL, and the only way to change the dates was the calendar's "a day earlier/later" buttons.

After: the trip's first and last day belong to the reader. You drag either end of the band on the year strip, step it with the arrow keys, or type the dates in the row beneath it. Clicking a festival fills in its run plus a day either side, and that festival leads the trip (theme, reach) while the trip still overlaps it. Otherwise the festival the trip covers most leads. The calendar plans every festival the dates reach. Either side of the dates is a flight block, one out and one home, with a plane icon. It shows the cheapest fare for that day (time, length, stops, price) linking to Aviasales, or Aviasales' search for the day when no fare is known. The "where are you coming from" question now sits under the dates, and the blocks can change the answer and take any airport code.

The fares come from a new Cloudflare Worker (`api/`), because the partner's API token is a secret the page must not hold. Everything else is still served straight from `site/`. With no token configured, the Worker answers an empty list, so until #876 is done the blocks show the search link.

How: `site/planNG/lib/trip.js` holds the trip rules (cap, order, which festival leads), `timeline-view.js` draws and drives the band handles, and `planNG.js` replaces the per-festival focus with `setTrip()`. `site/planNG/lib/flights.js` holds the airport, currency and fetch rules. `api/fares.js` calls Travelpayouts' `prices_for_dates` with the token in a header. The URL is now `?from=&to=` (plus `&festival=` while a chosen festival leads), and `?festival=` alone still opens that festival's run. `wrangler.jsonc` gains `main` and `run_worker_first: ["/api/*"]`. I checked this with `wrangler dev`: `/api/fares` answers, pages and data files are served, unknown paths get the 404 page, and `/planJerusalem/` still redirects with 301. A `--dry-run` deploy with the release's pinned `wrangler@4.128.0` bundles `api/index.js` (3 KB) beside the same 171-file `site/` upload, so the nightly release needs no change.

Spec: section 23 is rewritten for trip dates. 23.3 (the calendar-end buttons) is retired, and 23.8 and 23.9 are new. Section 27 (flights, 27.1 to 27.5) is new. The existing PlanNG goldens are re-baselined in the last commit, because the trip row now sits under the timeline and the period bar is gone from above the calendar. The calendar-only crops moved by a few pixels at most.

**Not verified:** the sandbox cannot reach Travelpayouts. So the reply shape `api/fares.js` parses, and the Aviasales search URL format, come from the partner's documentation and have not been checked against a live answer. The 27.5 sample is hand-written, and the spec says so. #876 covers the account, the token and the marker.

Builds on #874 (it removed the trip links and the origin line). This branch will be merged forward once #874 lands.

{"number":885,"title":"PlanNG: the questions become a slim chip row, with festival and kind filters","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ue?thread=cmsg_01KFmEpC61cnd1keNHYDR7ueE9Bu9ZnbTitrMTkGkfEXp4)_

Before: the four questions above the calendar were big cards whose height followed how many answers they held. With 25 kinds, "What are you here for?" was about 600px tall, and every "More" pushed the calendar further down. The kinds were each festival's own categories, and there was no way to filter by festival.

After: one slim row of chips sits above the calendar: festivals, kinds, pace, travel and food. Each chip shows its current answer and stays the same height whatever the answer is. Clicking a chip opens a panel that floats over the calendar with the picture answers and the exact numbers underneath, so the calendar never moves. A click outside the panel or Escape closes it.

- **Kinds** are now the same eight for every festival: film, comedy, theatre, dance, music, family, talk and other. These come from the data pipeline's own genre list, and Edinburgh's genres are mapped onto it. A kind is still a preference: it outranks the rest but never hides anything (21.3).
- **Tags:** under the kinds, each festival in the trip lists its own categories. Clicking a tag cycles through neutral, ✓ only these, and ⊘ not these. Tags are hard filters (21.12). The list scrolls, has a box to find a tag by name, and is capped at `FACET_OPTIONS`.
- **Festivals:** each festival in the trip gets a checkbox and its theme colour. A festival that is unticked drops all of its shows from the draft.

How: `site/planNG/lib/filters.js` holds the pure rules. `planNG.js` renders the chip row, filters the pool before drafting, and stores `festivalsOut` and `tags` alongside the other preferences. A stored interest that is an old category slug is dropped when read. `planNG.css` now names each festival's accent once (`--colour-<id>`). Each theme's `--violet` and the new festival dots both read it, so the dots are ready to reuse for the block stripes later. `PICK_CHIPS`, the "more kinds" chip, the expanders and the unused per-festival kind emoji are removed.

Spec: 21.1, 21.2 and 21.4 are reworded. 21.10 to 21.13 are new. The notes on 25.1 and the rows of the 26.1 table are updated.

Goldens: 21.1, 21.2, 21.4, 19.3 and 23.7 show the new row, and 21.11 and 21.13 are new. The other Jerusalem goldens that changed (18.x, 20.x, 21.5 to 21.8, and the full-page 19.1 and 19.2) differ only because the calendar now starts higher on the page. That shifts their crops by one pixel or a few rows, and their content is unchanged. I checked each against its old golden with a one-pixel shift allowed, and looked at 18.4 and 20.4 side by side.

Checked: `npm run verify` passes, and `npm run test:ui` passes twice in a row.

Builds on #875.

{"number":891,"title":"PlanNG: kept days, flight hours, and meals and personal time as blocks","body":"Before: the calendar had draggable first-night and last-night edges with FROM/TO flags, and a date window in the programme drawer. Meals were bands at the same hour every day. Nothing on the calendar knew about the flights, and a day could only hold shows.

After: clicking a day's head keeps that day for rest, an excursion, or a nearby festival, and every first draft keeps one such day. The Haifa trip gives a day to Acco, and the Jerusalem trip gets a rest day on the day that costs least. A kept day's block can be clicked to change or clear it, or dragged to another day. The cheapest flights block the first day until landing plus the trip from the airport, and the last day from when you have to leave for the airport. "How do you want to eat?" now puts a meal block on every day. Clicking an empty hour offers a meal named for that time of day (a snack if the day already has that meal) or personal time. These blocks can be dragged, stretched and removed. The edges and the drawer's date window are gone.

The draft engine takes a new `allowSlot` rule, so kept days and every block the reader places are respected the same way as the day's hours.

How: the pure rules live in `site/planNG/lib/days.js`. `seedDay` picks the kept day, `slotRule` says what the draft may not use, `flightHours` works in the festival's own time zone, and `mealAt` names a new meal. The page stores the reader's days under `planNG.days`, but only once the reader changes them, so on a first visit the page still stores nothing but its theme. Suggesting restaurants and bookings still needs a restaurant data source and a privacy update, so it isn't included.

Spec: new section 28 (28.1–28.8), 21.5 reworded, 21.8 retired. 22 existing goldens were re-rendered because the seeded rest day now falls on Mon 19 Oct in Jerusalem and Mon 10 Aug in Edinburgh. Four cases whose story happens on that Monday now start with the reader having cleared the kept day (`jerusalemAllDays()`), so their goldens stay the same. This PR also restores the fare service path in the fares banner (`api/fares.js`), which the earlier merge of #875 into the filter-bar branch had reverted.

{"number":893,"title":"PlanNG: who's coming fills in the questions you haven't answered","body":"Before: nothing asked who was coming, so every question started at the same default whether a family with a five-year-old was travelling or someone on their own.

After: "Who's coming?" is the first chip, with just me, a couple, family (with the children's ages, as on the Plan2 page) or friends. The answer fills in each question the reader hasn't answered themselves: how full a day is, which kinds are favoured, when the evening ends and how to eat. A filled-in chip shows its answer in italics with a ✨ marked "suggested". Once the reader answers a question, it's theirs, and changing who's coming no longer touches it.

Before: the page's colours jumped when a different festival took the lead, and each festival had its own palette. The year strip showed only festivals, today was a dashed line, and the trip's ends were small tabs. "Where are you coming to the festival from?" appeared under the dates on every first visit. The flight blocks always showed a plane and fetched fares for anyone coming from abroad.

After:
- **Genre colours that fade.** The colours come from the festival's genre (comedy, film, theatre, fringe), and switching festivals fades between them over about half a second. They switch at once when reduced motion is on.
- **Holiday orbs.** Each break the reader's public holidays make, counting the weekend and bridging a single work day, is a green orb on the months. An orb grows with the break's length (by its square root), not with the strip's scale. Pointing at one explains it, for example "Christmas Day · Boxing Day weekend, 25–28 Dec 2026 · 4 days off, Public holidays in United Kingdom". Until the reader answers, the country is guessed from their connection and the card says so.
- **Year strip.** Each end of the trip is a line across the strip with a grip in the middle, and the trip's length sits above the band. Today is a small stick figure on the months holding a "Today" sign. It shifts about a little and cheers whenever a choice is made, and holds still under reduced motion. Pointing at a festival shows its card: name, city and genre, dates and length, and whether its programme is out.
- **How you're getting here.** The blocks either side of the trip start dashed, with an icon that turns between a plane, a train and a car. Clicking one asks: "I live here", "I'll drive", "By train" or "I'm flying from" a country. Fares are fetched only for flying.

- **Palettes:** `data-genre` on the page root, taken from the registry's `kind`. The colour tokens are registered `<color>` properties that the root transitions.
- **Holidays:** `site/holidays/<CC>.json` holds 251 countries for 2026–2030 plus each country's own weekend, generated by `scripts/build-holidays.py`. `holidayBreaks()` in `site/planNG/lib/holidays.js` turns them into breaks. `/api/where` (`api/where.js`) returns only the edge's `request.cf.country` and is never cached; the privacy page says so.
- **Strip:** `site/planNG/timeline-view.js` draws the orbs, grips, figure and one shared hover card.
- **Arrival:** `site/planNG/lib/arrival.js` reads `arrive` on the stored origin, including answers saved before this change.

- New leaves: 23.10–23.14, section 29 (29.1–29.6), 24.6–24.8 and 27.6.
- Reworded leaves: 23.1, 23.6, 24.1, 27.1 and 27.4.
- 24.3 ("use my location") is retired.

{"number":896,"title":"Collect nine more festivals, the cities' sights, and the partner research","body":"Before: the festival planner knew the Fringe, Jerusalem, Acco and Haifa. It had no data on what else was on in Edinburgh in August, nothing about the cities themselves, and no record of which partners pay referrals.

After: nine more festivals are served. Brighton Fringe and Leicester Comedy come through Eventotron. The Edinburgh International Festival and the Book Festival come through Spektrix's open API, which includes seats available against capacity and full price lists. The Film Festival, the Tattoo (2027, because its ticketing API no longer lists 2026), the Art Festival, the Deaf Festival and Fringe by the Sea are also in. MICF and NZICF are placeholders. Six festival cities now have a sightseeing file with places, locations and opening hours that a planner can evaluate for any date. `product-wiki/partner-providers/` records which ticketing, hotel, travel, restaurant and tour providers pay referrals and have a queryable API.

One requirement case goes red on purpose. `fringe-scale.26.1` asserts that the Fringe planner pools 3,000–4,999 shows. It now pools 5,000, because the Edinburgh festivals that overlap the Fringe join the pool (3,984 Fringe + 1,016 others). Widening that assertion is the owner's call, so the case is left unchanged here.

How: platform code lives once under `scraper/festivals/platforms/`, with generic adapters under `scraper/convert/adapters/platforms/`. Fetches run six at a time, and cached pages refetch after six hours. A cold Brighton fetch dropped from 13m31s to 3m12s and EIF from 6m14s to 1m14s, with byte-identical raw output. `scraper/festivals/collect.py` runs one edition end to end. `scraper/cities/` fetches from OpenStreetMap and Wikidata and parses OSM opening hours into dated rules. Both drift checks and the self-tests run in `scripts/verify.sh`.

A short show at the end of the day was drawn past the day-end line, so it looked like the planner ignored the day's end. A show's popup opened the instant the pointer crossed a card and stayed open while the pointer wandered the calendar. Its four verdicts sat at the bottom as worded buttons, and the travel between shows and many controls explained themselves only in the browser's own tooltip.

After: every day runs from 08:00 to 01:00 at one fixed hour height, so moving the day's start or end never resizes the calendar. A big plus in the corner above the hours opens the night from 23:00 the evening before. The night starts folded, the page remembers the choice, and while folded the plus shows how many items the night holds. A block stops at the day-end line. A kept day's title ends in an ellipsis inside its column, and days in a row kept for the same thing join into one stretch under one title. Days keep their widths for the whole drag. Blocks slide to their new places, new ones grow in, and removed ones fade out where they stood; reduced motion skips all of it. The per-day count takes any number from zero up. The festivals chip marks each festival with the stripe its shows carry on the calendar and shows how far away it is. Festivals out of reach are listed there greyed out, and the lines above the calendar are gone.

Its four verdicts lead it as emoji (📌 lock this night, ❤️ favourite, 🔄 not this night, 👎 not this show), each named by the page's own tooltip on a rest of the pointer. Until the reader presses one, a hint under them says what they are for; a reader who already has verdicts never sees it. Resting on the travel between two shows opens a card: "Walking 7 minutes, from A, to B, 0.4 km, you arrive 23 min before the next show". No element on the planner carries a native `title` any more. A locked card's face mark is 📌 too, to match.

The block ceiling now includes the day end. The drag records which days were slivers when it began. The new `site/planNG/motion.js` snapshots the calendar before each redraw and plays the difference. `titleKeptRuns()` draws one title across a run of matching kept days. The new `site/planNG/tip.js` is the page's one tooltip for every `data-tip`; `wireCalendar()` adds the open and close timers, and `openLegPop()` shows a leg's card. {"number":903,"title":"Scrape the Acco festival from its real pages, and from Eventer","body":"The Acco data on `main` was never really scraped. Egress to both hosts was blocked when it landed, so both raw folders were transcribed from WebFetch summaries, and both parsers were written against reconstructed markup. Both hosts are reachable now, and a real fetch showed that the parsers misread the pages.

### 1. Parse the real programme pages
- **street-programme**: found 62 cards and **0 performances**. On the real page each day and its times sit in separate `<dt>`/`<dd>` cells, the title is the `<h3>` (with an English `<span>`), and the first line is a genre chip. The parser now reads that structure. It also keeps each card's blurb, picture, credits and English title. The raw shape changed, so `FETCHER_VERSION` is now 2.
- **acco-tc**: the parser put the hall inside a label (`כניסה חופשית (אולם הפואייה)`), kept `בכורה (לנשים בלבד)` as one label, and dropped the labels from lines marked "sold out". All three are fixed.
- Both `samples/programme.html` files are now the real pages as fetched on 2026-09-25, and the self-tests assert on them.

### 2. Eventer as a new source for the theatre programme
`eventer.co.il/user/accofestival` loads everything from one open JSON call (`/user/<user>/getData`), with one event per performance. It is fetched through a new shared platform module, `scraper/festivals/platforms/eventer.py`. Eventer never adds a performance. Each Eventer event is matched to the programme line with the same date and start time. When two lines share a time slot, the ticket link decides.

| fact | winner |
|---|---|
| title, labels, schedule, free concerts | acco-tc |
| hall, running time | Eventer title line, e.g. `האולם האדום (50 דק')` |
| prices | Eventer: full price and concessions. The Akko residents' rate needs ID and stays in `ticketing`. The couple ticket is a price for two seats and is left out. |
| ticket link, availability | Eventer, then acco-tc's sold-out marks, because Eventer drops a performance once it sells out |
| blurb, picture | Eventer |

Result: all 22 ticketed performances now have a hall, a running time, prices, a blurb and a picture. Before this, none of them had any of these.

Two data-level calls to review:
- The programme page lists 29.9 20:00 אורשינא, but its link points to the **28.9** Eventer performance, and Eventer has no 29.9 performance. The line is kept, with no ticket link and `status: unknown`.
- acco-tc no longer emits `null` blurb, duration or image. A `null` counts as supplying the field in the merge, so it would have beaten Eventer's values.

### Verification
- `npm run verify` is green: parse self-tests on the real pages, `eventer.py --selftest`, and `to_serving --check`.
- `npm run test:ui`: 183 of 183 pass.
- Served `site/` and opened `/planNG?festival=acco`. No page errors, and Acco shows now carry running times (e.g. "עדן מאבא עבור … 50 min").

# The data pipeline

The API's field reference is `scraper/SCRAPING.md` and the file layout `scraper/README.md`; this
is the judgment those two don't carry.

## Verifying a change

- **Verifying a scraper change against the live API** — only a sanctioned task drives the
  API: `full-scrape`, `fetch-prices`, `price-probe`, `refresh-shows` or `refresh-tickets`. Never
  "verify" by reasoning about what the API probably returns; have a task run it, or say plainly
  it is unverified.

- **Answering a one-off API question** (a field's shape, an enum's values, whether an operation
  exists) — `scraper/SCRAPING.md` first; past it, `www.edfringe.com`'s Next.js bundles carry
  the client's full GraphQL operation set (recipe in SCRAPING.md), where the probe shows the host
  reachable. That shows what a query looks like, never what it returns, so a change checked only
  that way is still unverified. Past that, ask the owner.

- **Changing the normalizer** — `python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform
  check that runs offline (raw → master → day file → `shows.min.json` on a fixture). Run it.

## Tickets and prices

- **Writing availability logic, client or scraper** — key off the per-performance
  `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` with nothing to
  sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). `SOLD_OUT` and `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` are
  unavailable, everything else available, unknown available (`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in
  `site/js/app.js`). `soldOut` is carried for display only.

- **Pricing a show** — price every performance, not one per show: previews sell cheaper and
  weekends dearer, and pricing one performance published 28% of shows at their cheapest night.
  No "skip previews" heuristic fixes that; GraphQL aliases carry a whole run per request
  (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), and there is no call budget to economise against.

- **Choosing which price a payload carries** — `shows.min.json` (planner) answers "what does
  this show cost?" with the run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax`; `site/data/days/*.json` (Now page)
  answers "what does it cost tonight?" with that performance's own `pm`. A performance the cache
  has no entry for gets no `pm` at all ("Price TBC"), never a neighbouring night's figure or the
  show's minimum.

- **Handling a show with no price** — it is a normal, permanent state: `data/prices.json` is a
  fetch-once cache off the nightly path, and `refresh-shows` carries its amounts through without
  re-fetching. Keep both cache entry shapes readable (current `sets` + `perfs`, legacy bare
  `min`/`max`; `price_sets` reads both); dropping the legacy shape or emptying the cache blanks
  prices until a full pass finishes.

- **Encoding a price at any stage** — keep three states, never two:

  | state | master | wire |
  |---|---|---|
  | costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
  | priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
  | unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |

  Never encode unknown as `0` or let a decoder default it to one. `priceMin: 0` and `free: true`
  are separate claims (the flag is the listing's, the £0 can be the price API's); the price path
  keys off `priceMin` and `free` stays what the listing said. What the site shows for an unknown
  price is a product decision in `site/shared/price.js`.

- **Reading the raw price payload** — amounts arrive as strings, and nearly every show carries a
  £0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession that is never the cheapest price (SCRAPING.md's pricing
  section).

## Time

- **Reading a performance's `dateTime` from the listing API** — it is a real UTC instant, not
  Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`; slicing its digits is an hour wrong all August. The
  pipeline crosses the zone once, in `normalize.local_date_start`, shared by
  `refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py`. Everything written after it is Edinburgh
  wall-clock, so no stage downstream parses, converts or re-offsets a time.

- **Comparing "now" against performance times** — read now in Edinburgh too,
  `site/js/clock.js`'s `festivalNow` / `festivalDate`, never the device clock: a UK visitor can't
  see the difference, a visitor from another zone gets the whole drift. (now-compared-against)

- **Changing the time-zone conversion** — it is a full-snapshot change: rebuild the master
  through the new conversion and regenerate every derived artifact. Expect performances to move
  between day files (late 31 Aug ones fall into 1 Sep, outside the August day files) rather than
  reading that as data loss. (conversion-change-full)

## Committed data and caching

- **Fixing wrong data under `data/normalized/` or `site/data/`** — fix `scraper/normalize.py`
  and re-run it (`--merge` to top up, no flag for a full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit
  is overwritten by the next `refresh-shows` and leaves the bug in the generator.
  `data/prices.json` is committed input written by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`, and nothing
  overwrites a hand-edit there, which is why re-running the fetch is the only fix.

- **Adding a festival, an edition or a source** — `site/data/festivals/` is
  `scraper/convert/to_serving.py`'s output and `data/festivals/` its hand-fetched input; name each
  new file and its writer in `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output`'s allowlist, never the
  directory.

- **Writing a job that commits generated data and can run over an hour** — its push is
  guaranteed to be rejected by the hourly ticket refresh, so on rejection re-derive rather than
  merge: fetch `origin/main`, take its generated files, regenerate from that master plus the
  job's own input, retry. Call `commit_regenerated` in the task workers' `worker-lib.sh`, which
  does exactly that.

- **Changing anything that moves a performance's join key** (venue + date + time) — the
  browser caches `shows.min.json` and `availability.min.json` separately and joins them by that
  key, so a generation split breaks the join while both files are fresh by TTL.
  `join_fingerprint(master)` in `normalize.py`, mirrored as `joinFingerprint()` in
  `site/plan/lib/hydrate.js` and carried as the sidecar's `k`, is how `plan.js` detects the split
  and evicts both. Keep the two implementations agreeing (the self-test asserts it); a TTL bump
  doesn't cover this.

## The wire format

- **Adding or dropping an indexed wire field** — the day files and `shows.min.json` reference
  `site/data/venues.json`'s lists by position (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`,
  `ar`), with one producer and two decoders that change in the same commit: `scraper/normalize.py`
  (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` / `minify_master` / `build_availability`),
  `site/js/app.js` `adaptShow`, and `site/plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`.
  `edfringe-lookup-indices` catches an unresolved index but not a decoder reading the old key, so
  check both decoders by hand.

- **Changing a lookup list** — append only (`extend_lookup`), never reorder or drop: the browser
  decodes a days-old catalogue against a newer `venues.json`, and a moved entry relabels shows
  with no error anywhere. (lookup-lists-append)

- **Putting anything that changes through the day into `shows.min.json`** — don't: ticket status
  lives in `availability.min.json` so `refresh-tickets` rewrites it alone; in the catalogue it
  would tie that bulky download to the refresh and freeze availability in cached copies.
  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`. (shows-min-json)

- **Adding a plain wire key** (such as `pm` / `px`) — the same three files move, and the new key
  sits at the same position in `normalize_event`'s dict and `rehydrateShows`'s object literal:
  the round-trip test compares as JSON, so a key-order mismatch fails it and reads like a data

3:description: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
50:There's no cost to a branch carrying many commits when the project uses a **squash** merge to `main` (one commit per PR): the squash collapses them into a single commit on `main`, so `main`'s one-commit-per-PR history is unaffected no matter how granularly the branch is committed.
52:- **One caveat, at merge time: before rebasing an *unmerged* multi-commit branch onto a *moved* base, collapse commits that rewrite the same lines into one.** When your own commits churn the same lines (build X → refactor → remove X, common in an iterative design session) and the base has advanced, rebasing the stack replays *every* intermediate conflict against the new base. The squash-merge discards those commits anyway, so collapse them first — `git reset --soft $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)` then one fresh commit, and rebase that single commit: one conflict pass, not N. Lossless (unlike `reset --hard` + redo) and simpler than `--onto` when you want a single commit anyway.
54:- **When a rebase or a review round drops part of a branch, amend the commit message in the same step** — then read it back against `git show --stat` before merging. Under a squash merge the branch's commit body *becomes* `main`'s permanent record, while the explanation of what was dropped, if it lives in a PR comment, is not carried by the squash at all. A commit describing a change to files it never touched sends the next reader of `git log -- <path>` hunting for work that isn't there.
57:- **Fixing a trailer or arming auto-merge on a branch already pushed - add a commit, don't force-push.** The session's own permission classifier can deny `git push --force-with-lease` outright as a destructive rewrite of an already-pushed commit, even for the smallest edit, and a differently-phrased retry hits the same classifier. Skip the amend: make a new commit (`--allow-empty` if nothing in the tree actually changed) and push it as a plain fast-forward - it carries the fix forward with no force-push in the loop at all.
59:- After your commit is **squash-merged** to `main`, a *reused* feature branch still carries that original commit (the squash created a *new* commit on `main`, so the branch's own is unreachable from it) — and the next PR off the branch re-includes it in the diff, because the three-dot merge-base predates the squash. Sync the branch to `origin/main` before opening the next PR (`git rebase origin/main`, which drops the commit as an already-applied cherry-pick, or a hard reset): it's your own un-merged branch, so this is the amend-your-own-commits case above, not rewriting shared history.
60:  - **`git rebase origin/main` only drops the old commit cleanly when the branch carried a *single* squash-merged commit.** When it carried *several* commits that `main` squashed into *one* (then kept developing), git can't match them to the squash as already-applied, so it replays them and conflicts mid-rebase. Replant only the genuinely-new commits instead: `git rebase --onto origin/main <last-squash-merged-commit>` (then `git push --force-with-lease`). If the new work is small, a `git reset --hard origin/main` + redo beats fighting the replay.
84:Conflict size scales with how long a branch lives and how far it drifts from the default branch. Sync early rather than at the end: when starting work on a branch — and periodically while it's open — bring the latest default branch in first, so the branch carries current sources instead of discovering the gap at merge time. A one-commit-per-PR squash history already keeps each branch a single reviewable unit, so shorter-lived, freshly-synced branches are the norm.
86:**In a repo that forbids merge commits on the branch — the `squash-merge-history` check, or squash-only merging generally — sync by *rebasing*, never `git merge` the base in.** A `git merge origin/main` (even just to resolve conflicts) leaves a **merge commit** the check blocks, forcing a redo; `git pull --rebase` / `git rebase origin/main` replays your work with no merge commit. GitHub's **"Update branch"** button — and the `update_pull_request_branch` API behind it — is this same base-merge in disguise: it adds exactly the merge commit the check blocks, so refresh with a local rebase + `git push --force-with-lease` instead. The merge-conflict-resolution gotchas below apply to a rebase's conflicts exactly the same way.
108:The same fix, for a worse version of the same mistake: never branch from the bare local `main` (`git checkout -b <branch> main` / `git branch <branch> main`) in a checkout nothing keeps current — a long-lived clone in an unattended agent's workspace can sit with local `main` pinned at whatever commit it was cloned at, arbitrarily stale rather than merely one merge behind, because nothing ever fast-forwards a ref nobody checks into. `git fetch origin main` first, then branch from `origin/main` explicitly, every time — not only right after a merge you just watched happen.
120:## In a squash-merge repo, "commits ahead of main" does not mean "unmerged"
122:A squash-merge creates a new commit on `main` that the branch's own commits are unreachable from, so a branch whose work has already landed still shows ahead by N. **"Ahead by N" never alone means unmerged.** Determine real status by content, not raw count:
125:2. **Content diff** — `git diff --stat main..branch`: if everything the branch adds is already in `main`, the work landed (catches a squash with no surviving PR).
150:An automated or scheduled job that derives its branch name from a non-unique key (e.g. the date) collides with itself on a repeat run for that key — `git checkout -b` fails when the branch already exists, and a push to the diverged remote branch is rejected non-fast-forward (so the run can't even open its PR). Give every run its own branch: append a per-run-unique suffix (`$RANDOM` / a short token) to the readable prefix.
156:When the escalation is itself a separate reusable workflow invoked via `workflow_call`, permissions don't propagate implicitly through the chain: the job that calls it needs the permission explicitly granted (e.g. `issues: write`), and if that reusable workflow in turn calls another one, the middle workflow must forward the same grant to its own call — a caller two levels up granting it once is not enough.
184:Its `merged`/`merged_at` fields can read `false`/empty for a PR that has genuinely landed by squash-merge, even with `fields` narrowed. Confirm landed-ness by grepping the base branch's commit subjects for the squash's `(#N)`, or call `pull_request_read` `get` on the one PR you care about.

---
name: requirements-harness
description: How EdFringeNow runs product/requirements.md as tests under a real headless Chromium - writing leaves and goldens, the harness's determinism traps, the frozen fixtures and golden approval. Use before editing product/requirements.md or anything under product/requirements/.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
    - "product/requirements.md"
    - "product/requirements/**"
---

# The requirements harness

The framework conventions are the `executable-requirements` pack and the judgment layer is
`spec-driven-product` plus the `writing-tests` skill; layout, lanes and commands are
`product/requirements/README.md`. This carries what those don't: a Playwright golden harness,
and the local approval and fixture policy.

## Writing the spec

- **Laying out `product/requirements.md`** — under each visual leaf its golden is visible and
  uncollapsed; every textual expansion (acceptance notes, proof pointers) is collapsed in a
  `<details>` block. The document is read by sight.

- **Writing a visual leaf's statement** — one line saying what is asserted; the golden carries
  the copy, counts, colours and placement. Anything not visible (a threshold, the rule behind
  the state) goes in a collapsed **Notes** block. (visual-leafs-statement)

- **Choosing a golden's capture** — the smallest surface that proves the leaf: an element crop,
  a clipped region, or a stitched composite, never the whole page or control. The recipe lives on
  the case (`capture: "<selector>"` or `capture(page, tools)`, see `shared/capture-tools.js`);
  whole-page capture is a deliberate exception. (golden-smallest-surface)

- **Proving what an action changes** — capture the same region before and after (and after a
  reload where persistence is the point) and play them as one animated golden (`tools.animate`);
  keep `stitchV`/`stitchH` for things genuinely side by side. (change-time-animation)

- **Encoding an animated golden** — APNG, never GIF (`shared/png.js`'s `encodeAnimated`); the
  comparator compares an animated golden's bytes only. (animated-golden-apng)

- **Placing a leaf both pages follow** — the spec is organised by what the product does, never by
  code layout: a cross-page rule is one feature whose picture shows both the Now page and the
  planner, in the cross-page part after the two page-by-page segments. A case may navigate
  between pages, or open a second page when something fixed at context creation must differ.

- **About to route a leaf to `behavior` or `logic`** — first ask whether it decomposes into
  observable states; a statement joined by "and" usually does, and each part becomes its own
  numbered sub-leaf with its own picture, the parent a heading. When a leaf lands in a coded kind
  because the product makes it invisible, say so in its Notes and name the product change that
  would make it visual.

- **Using `behavior`** — for a gesture's outgoing consequence (a URL built, bytes downloaded,
  storage written) or what the OS paints rather than the page (a native `title` tooltip, a
  cursor). (behavior-rule)

- **Using `logic`** — for a pure rule with no rendered surface; when it is about how values are
  written, declare `table: { columns, rows }` so the gallery renders the table and `verify()`
  proves every row. (logic-rule)

## The browser is part of the expected

- **Bumping the pinned Playwright** — it re-renders every golden, so it is a re-baselining,
  approved like one: the harness refuses any other version (`shared/harness/browser.js`).

- **A comparison that flaps** — add determinism, never a tolerance; the comparator stays at zero
  diff, and the levers (fixed clock, geolocation, seeded `Math.random`, route-fulfilled network,
  frozen animations, render flags) all live in the harness.

## Traps the harness already paid for

- **Serving the fake origin** — keep it `https://`: geolocation exists only on secure origins,
  and on plain http the app keeps its simulated clock and renders the wrong day.
  (geolocation-exists-only)

- **Moving or denying the fixed geolocation** — the app adopts the device clock only on an
  in-UK fix, so anywhere else renders its pre-set simulated moment, a different day file.
  (app-adopts-device)

- **Captures racing the planner's board animation** — a CSS freeze doesn't stop
  `element.animate`; the harness stubs it to land on end states. (css-freeze-does)

- **Text shifting by a pixel everywhere** — the vendored `fonts.css` resolves against
  `fonts.googleapis.com`, so the vendor route matches on path, host-agnostic. (fonts-arrive-google)

- **Adding an emoji, symbol or script to the product or fixtures** — rebuild the
  `harness/vendor/systemfonts/` subset (its README): Chromium runs under a `FONTCONFIG_FILE`
  that sees only that directory, and a missing glyph renders as tofu. (vendoring-web-fonts)

- **Reproducing a golden flake locally** — compare with the harness's `compare.js`, never a byte
  hash: PNG bytes differ across identical renders, and CI enforces pixels.
  (reproducing-golden-flake)

- **A red `ui-requirements` lane** — its artifact downloads from a host the proxy denies, so read
  which case failed from `get_job_logs` (large `tail_lines`) and re-run it locally;
  `npm run test:ui` writes `.actual.png` / `.diff.png` into `shared/.artifacts/`. (red-ci-lanes)

- **Capturing a floating popup** — set `viewportOnly: true`: a full-page capture scrolls, and
  scrolling dismisses tips, legends and pops. (floating-popup-dies)

- **Waiting for a page to be ready** — wait on the observable state the pages settle into (the
  footer version popup's text, the search placeholder's show count; `case-helpers.js`) plus
  `document.fonts.ready`, never `networkidle`. (ready-networkidle)

- **Capturing hover-driven UI** — open it inside `capture()`, not `drive()`: the runner settles
  the scroll between them, and the scroll fires `mouseleave`. (hover-driven-ui)

## The fixture freeze

- **Needing data for a case** — use `shared/fixtures/data/`, a frozen snapshot of the real
  committed data cast by the committed builder for state variety; never reach for `site/data/`.
  Every deviation from the source bytes is an `ADJUST` in the builder.

- **Re-running the builder** — it re-casts every golden, so run it only with the owner's
  approval and land builder, fixtures, goldens and gallery in one reviewed change.

- **Having invoked `build-fixtures.js` at all**, even against a scratch edit — it writes into
  `fixtures/data/` as it goes, so `git diff --stat` the whole fixtures dir before deciding there
  is nothing to revert. (build-fixtures-partial-drift)

## Golden approval

- **A golden that no longer matches** — show the owner the committed golden beside
  `shared/.artifacts/<case>.actual.png` and `.diff.png` through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, one
  per item, and say so in the PR body.

- **Landing an intended UI change** — spec edit (doc-first, red), then the implementation, then
  `npm run refresh:ui`, with the refreshed PNGs in the same diff.

    * PlanNG: city pills, a draggable trip, and travel pictures beside it
    
    A city's festivals that run together share one pill: each run a shade inside
    it, the country's flag at its middle, labelled with how many there are and
    the one with a programme and the longest run, which choosing the pill picks.
    The band drags as a whole, keeping its length and the festival chosen, and a
    press that never moves is still a click. Each end names its day of the month.
    
    The dates row and flight blocks under the strip are gone. A lane under the
    pills holds the grips and a large picture beside each end, changing between
    plane, train, car and house until the reader says where they live (their
    connection's country filled in) and how they travel; after that it holds
    still and opens the travel card, which carries the flights and the airport.
    A picture with no room before the strip's edge is left out.
    
    The genre washes are deeper and the city photograph stronger, so a change of
    festival reads as a change of place.

own page, and carries event pictures too. Cinema Reshet, the outdoor
shorts venue, gets a curated entry. The self-test runs on captured pages.

* PlanNG: the show popup leads with its picture

Hovering a show now opens its picture from the festival's own site, then its
name, venue and time, four lines of its description with a link to the
festival's page, and the nights and verdicts as before. A show with no
picture, or one that fails to load, shows its kind's emoji on its festival's
colour. The popup sits beside the card instead of over it, clear of the
sticky header. The catalogue now carries each show's image, the privacy page
says pictures load from festival sites, and the test harness serves one
stand-in photo for the festival image hosts.

[{"sha":"7cd4cdeb0e936124bacd4ee18b27644a1b5ed987","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/7cd4cdeb0e936124bacd4ee18b27644a1b5ed987","message":"PlanNG: keep the site header the same for every festival

The top bar no longer changes with the focused festival: the logo is always
EdFringeNow, the nav's third link always reads Festivals, the city-and-dates
hint is gone, and the bar keeps the house palette (opaque, so the festival's
wash does not tint it). Which festival the page plans is left to the timeline
and the page title. Spec 18.1 and 23.6 rewritten to match; goldens refreshed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01E77Vq2uqKwAq59UVUKTiqS","author":{"name":"Claude","email":"noreply@anthropic.com","date":"2026-09-24T17:41:57Z"}},{"sha":"6de9c9584cf87e296e86f1e41e05f3e3bde14ccb","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/6de9c9584cf87e296e86f1e41e05f3e3bde14ccb","message":"PlanNG: remove the trip links and export buttons from the page

The "While you're here" partner links, the CSV and ICS export buttons and
their note are gone from the calendar card, along with the origin line that
lived inside the trip links and the footer's partner-link disclosure, which
no longer has links to disclose. The trip-link builder and the export module
stay, so the features can be placed again: 18.6, 18.7 and 24.2 now prove the
builder as logic leaves, and 24.5 carries the asked-once half of the old
24.2. Strings nothing draws are removed or marked unrendered; goldens that
move with the shorter page are refreshed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01E77Vq2uqKwAq59UVUKTiqS","author":{"name":"Claude","email":"noreply@anthropic.com","date":"2026-09-24T17:56:58Z"}},{"sha":"312ce40157d5d2c7263fcb17234c099c8ffe9853","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/312ce40157d5d2c7263fcb17234c099c8ffe9853","message":"Spec: the trip's dates are the reader's, and flights either side of them

Section 23 now makes the timeline set the trip's first and last day (dragged
or typed), with a festival a shortcut to its run; 23.3's calendar-end buttons
retire. Section 27 adds the flight blocks either side of the dates.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GjDQR2zHUeyKV4dM4mgpoP","author":{"name":"Claude","email":"noreply@anthropic.com","date":"2026-09-24T17:59:20Z"}},{"sha":"57a737471953d41431e67a592370a215ef14c219","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/57a737471953d41431e67a592370a215ef14c219","message":"Fare service: a Worker that asks the flight partner for one day's cheapest fares

The partner's token is a secret, so the page cannot ask it directly: api/
answers /api/fares server-side and the rest of the site is still served
straight from site/. With no token configured it answers an empty list.
The Aviasales links (search and per-fare) join the other partner links in
site/shared/affiliates.js, and the privacy page now says what the lookup
sends.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GjDQR2zHUeyKV4dM4mgpoP","author":{"name":"Claude","email":"noreply@anthropic.com","date":"2026-09-24T18:20:48Z"}},{"sha":"674588388172209daa70c5afba3c4393e26c33d7","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/674588388172209daa70c5afba3c4393e26c33d7","message":"PlanNG: the reader sets the trip's dates on the year strip, with flights either side

The band on the timeline is the trip: drag its ends, step them with the arrow
keys, or type the dates beneath it. Clicking a festival fills in its run and
a day either side and leads the trip while the trip reaches it; otherwise the
festival the trip covers most leads. Every festival the dates reach is
planned. Either side of the dates sits a flight block, which carries the
where-from question and shows the cheapest fare out and home, or the
partner's search for the day. The calendar's own day-earlier/later buttons
retire.

product-wiki/partner-providers/ surveys which ticketing, hotel, transport,
restaurant and excursion providers pay referrals and expose an API a planner
can query with what it knows about a visitor. No festival box office runs an
affiliate scheme; referral income is in non-festival events (Skiddle,

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GpVuqLmQaSXDxpeef5n3SP","author":{"name":"Claude","email":"noreply@anthropic.com","date":"2026-09-25T14:33:46Z"}},{"sha":"ad4dc180977012ae5cafcb2442140e4ecf761460","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/ad4dc180977012ae5cafcb2442140e4ecf761460","message":"Collect nine more festivals through shared platform fetchers

Brighton Fringe and Leicester Comedy Festival (Eventotron), the Edinburgh
International Festival and Book Festival (Spektrix's open API, with seats
available of capacity and price lists), the Film Festival, the Tattoo (its
ticketing API; 2027, since the API no longer lists 2026), the Art Festival,
the Deaf Festival and Fringe by the Sea. MICF and NZICF are placeholders
whose not-built fetchers record what was probed.

Platform code lives once under scraper/festivals/platforms/ with generic
adapters under scraper/convert/adapters/platforms/. Requests go through
common.fetch_all (six at a time) and cached pages refetch after six hours;
busy answers retry, honouring Retry-After. A cold Brighton fetch went from
13m31s to 3m12s, EIF from 6m14s to 1m14s, with byte-identical raw.
collect.py runs an edition's sources and conversion in one command.

For each festival city, scraper/cities/ fetches the museums, galleries,
gardens, parks, markets, viewpoints and landmarks from OpenStreetMap, ranks
them by their Wikipedia editions via Wikidata, and serves
site/data/cities/<city>.json with each place's location and its opening hours
parsed into dated rules a planner can evaluate for any day (seasonal hours
included; unparsed stays null). Where OSM has no hours for an Edinburgh
highlight, curated/edinburgh.json carries them from the official page.

Slice covered: PRs #897, #895, #898, #903, #900, #902, #901, #904, #905. All are single-session agent PRs merged directly by the owner with zero PR comments/reviews on any of them (`get_comments` and `get_reviews` returned `[]` for every one) — so the only source material is the commit diffs/bodies themselves, not review back-and-forth.

Two candidates cleared the bar; everything else was either a one-off UI/product decision, already covered by an existing rule/skill, or too thin to generalize.

**Candidate 1 — repeated scraper onboarding failure**
- Rule: "Adding a scraper for a new external festival source while its site is unreachable — don't write the parser, or commit its sample fixtures/self-test, against markup reconstructed from a WebFetch summary; land it provisional and re-parse from a real fetch once the host is reachable, rather than treating the reconstruction as done."
- Evidence: #903 body — "The Acco data on `main` was never really scraped. Egress to both hosts was blocked when it landed, so both raw folders were transcribed from WebFetch summaries, and both parsers were written against reconstructed markup. Both hosts are reachable now, and a real fetch showed that the parsers misread the pages." #904 body, independently, same window — "The Haifa parser was written against pages reconstructed from summaries, and the first real fetch showed where they differed." Both required near-full parser rewrites once real access arrived.
- Why it clears the bar: it recurred twice in the same window across two unrelated festival sources (Acco, Haifa), so it's a repeated gotcha, not a one-off; it's specific to this repo's practice of onboarding new `scraper/festivals/platforms/*` sources under egress constraints, distinct from the generic canon `fetching-from-the-web` rule ("a summarizing fetch tool is not a source") which the sessions apparently already knew and still fell into this pattern at the commit/fixture level, not just the in-chat-answer level.
- Landing mechanism: prose in the `data-pipeline` skill's existing scraper-verification section (sits right next to "Verifying a scraper change against the live API — only a sanctioned task drives the API… have a task run it, or say plainly it is unverified"). Not a check — nothing structural distinguishes a reconstructed sample from a real one.

**Candidate 2 — leftover pointer triggers an unintended tooltip in a capture**
- Rule: "After driving a click/drag that reflows the layout, move the pointer off before capturing — the reflow can leave it resting on an element whose own hover-tip then renders over the shot, non-deterministically (fine locally, different in CI)."
- Evidence: #900, code comment — `// Off the fare, whose own label would otherwise open over the picture.` before `page.mouse.move(0, 0)`; and its commit body — "The next contender slides under the pointer after the click and, depending on timing, reopens a popup over the hour, so the golden rendered one way locally and another in CI." #901, same pattern twice — `// Off the button, whose own label would otherwise open over the days.`
- Why it clears the bar: appeared 3 times across 2 separate PRs, is a distinct failure mode from the already-landed `hover-driven-ui` rule (that one is about scroll-triggered `mouseleave` between `drive()`/`capture()`; this is about a *leftover* hover-tip appearing after an unrelated click/drag, fixed by parking the pointer at `(0,0)`), and would save a future case-author a CI flake round-trip.
- Landing mechanism: one bullet in the `requirements-harness` skill's "Traps the harness already paid for" list, alongside `hover-driven-ui`/`floating-popup-dies`.

**Dropped, not reported:**
- #905 (cursor revert to browser default) — pure product/design decision (owner's stated cursor preference), and its one non-obvious CSS technique (`cursor: revert !important` scoped to `.festival-page` rather than editing the shared `plan.css`) is already explained inline as a code comment at its one call site — not a generalizable rule.
- #897, #895, #898, #902 — clean single-shot feature PRs, no rework, no reviewer pushback, nothing beyond what the harness/data-pipeline skills already cover (e.g. #902's `// Opened inside capture()` comment is just an application of the already-landed `hover-driven-ui` rule, not a new one).

Reviewed all 9 PRs (#874, #875, #885, #891, #893, #892, #894, #890, #896): full diffs via `git show`, plus `pull_request_read` get/get_comments/get_reviews for each. None carry human review — every PR is a single-author, self-merged agent PR with zero review comments and zero review threads (only two self-authored CI-status comments, on #890 and #896). So the richest source here is PR bodies, commit-by-commit history within each squash, and diffs — not review dialogue.

One candidate clears the bar:

**Rule candidate:** "Testing a CSS-transition-driven value (a color, size, etc.) — never sample it at one fixed-delay point after the triggering change, even if gated on a `waitFor` of the state change itself; sample every frame across a bounded window from the change until the transition must be over, and assert some sampled frame lies strictly between the start/end values."

- **Source:** PR #890 (`a2491f8153b4057cdf4dec4e04d6abb1b5a906b4`), case `planng-theme-fade.23.10.case.js`, two commits within the same PR:
  - commit `159810f8`: first fix attempt — replaced a bare `page.waitForTimeout(150)` with `waitForFunction(() => ...dataset.festival === "haifa-iff")` + `waitForTimeout(100)`.
  - commit `dd798c98` (merge commit body): *"The 23.10 fade case now samples every frame of the fade rather than one moment, which a loaded machine could miss."* — replaced the single-sample approach entirely with a `MutationObserver` + `requestAnimationFrame` loop collecting every background-color frame for 900ms, then asserting `frames.some(c => c !== jerusalem && c !== haifa)`.

- Rule: strengthens the existing "Polling with an `until` loop" bullet — never re-poll a task you launched with `run_in_background: true`; wait for its notification instead of a second `until pgrep …; do sleep 10; done` foreground wrapper.
- Source, measured: PR #896 (session `b7a653f6…`, scraper `cities/fetch.py` background run). content.text: Confirmed: `declared-checks.json` at the pack root is auto-discovered, no wiring needed. Now let me check the required check-authoring workflow (red-first fixture test) and the `changing-pack-elements` / `writing-pack-prose` skills before landing anything.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/changing-pack-elements

# Changing a pack's elements

A pack's carriers - the rules in `RULES.md`, a skill and its triggers, a coded or declared
check, a task and its policy, the manifest - say *what* a session does. The decision behind
each - why it reads so, who decided, from what evidence, why this carrier and this trigger,
what was rejected, what would retire it - is one append-only file per element under the
pack's `provenance/`, read by maintenance and never by a session. Three things follow for
any edit under a pack.

## 1. The edit owes an entry, in the same change

Every change to what a carrier decides lands with an entry on the element's file, and the
`provenance-change-recorded` check says so again at the Stop hook when it did not. Which
file: the marker that ends a rule or guideline names it (`(url-filter-host-operators)` →
`provenance/url-filter-host-operators.md`), and two carriers may name one file while their
history is one; an unmarked guideline's is its skill's; a skill's is its directory name; a
check's its id with `/` as `-`; a task's its id; the manifest's `_pack.md`. Which kind:

| The change | Kind |
|---|---|
| a rule, guideline, skill body or step reads differently | `reworded` - or `strengthened` / `weakened` when the modality moved |
| a rule split in two, or two folded into one | `split` / `merged` (an entry on every file involved) |
| a guideline given a file of its own, its history having diverged from its skill's | `split` on the skill's file, `born` on the bullet's, with `Mechanism` |
| a rule moved to another carrier or pack | `moved`, with `Mechanism` |
| prose turned into a check | `converted`, with `Mechanism` and the deletion-test verdict |
| a skill's description or `force-load-on-*` trigger | `trigger-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a task's preconditions, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`, model or worker | `policy-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a check's severity, or the gate deciding when it fires | `severity-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| what an element applies to, where its text reads the same - a manifest's `requires` or fingerprint, a check's file scope, a skill's corpus | `scope-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a new element | `born`, with `Mechanism` - and `mark` first if the carrier has no file |
| an element removed | `retired` - the file stays, and this is its last entry |
| a review that found new evidence or changed the retire test | `reaffirmed`; a review that found nothing new writes nothing |

No entry is owed for whitespace, a re-wrap, a code comment in a check, a fixture, a test, a
README row, a version bump, or the marking pass's own markers and `body:` lines.

Write the entry in the file grammar and append it through the tool, which validates it and
refuses one that carries a secret:

```
node packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs append <pack> <element> <<'EOF'
## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the consequence clause said why twice (#2210)
- **Reason:** the second sentence restated the rule; cut.
- **Actor:** @handle (owner).
- **Model:** <the model this session runs, as the harness names it>
- **Landed:** #2210
EOF
```

In a member the tool is `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs`, and
the pack is under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. `--changed` in place of the element appends the
same entry to every element the working tree's diff touched - a sweep's one-line entries.
The fields, each written only where there is something behind it: `Source`, `Reason`,
`Actor` (the person by handle with their role, or the run and who merged it - never an
email), `Model`, `Mechanism` (the carrier and its trigger, and why - required on `born`,
`converted`, `moved`, `trigger-changed`, `policy-changed`, `severity-changed`), `Rejected`,
`Retire when`, `Landed`. An entry never restates the rule: the carrier is the description,
the entry is the decision. A candidate turned down goes on `_declined.md` the same way, kind
`declined`, with `Source`, `Reason` and `Actor`.

**Size the entry to the decision, never to the work.** Most are three to five lines. Each
field is the shortest answer that is still an answer, and one clause is usually the whole of
one - `Reason: the folder never existed.` Where a required `Mechanism` keeps the carrier it
already had, the new value is the whole of it - `a regex` - and the why-clause is owed only
where the choice of carrier was itself the decision. The diff, the commit message and the
pull request already hold what changed, how it was proved and what it cost; an entry
retelling any of them writes the record twice and buries the line a review came for. Length
is earned only by a decision that was weighed - an alternative turned down, a constraint that
forced the shape - so a corrected path, a repointed pattern or a renamed field gets one line,
and a change nobody deliberated over gets `Reason` alone. Cut a field rather than pad it, and
cut one that repeats another field or the entry's own title.

A file is meant to grow: a wrong entry is answered by a later one, never by editing the one
that was wrong. The check advises against a line lost or altered and refuses nothing.

### The one lane that writes the past

`append` and `apply` are append-only, and the tool enforces it: an entry dated before the
file's last is refused, because a change being recorded now cannot have happened before the
change recorded last. **The backfill is the deliberate exception**, and `--backfill` on
either command is how it says so. It is deriving a history that already happened, so its
entries are dated in the past by definition, and under that flag the file is re-rendered in
date order rather than appended to. Two things only it may do:

- **Replace what the references conversion wrote.** A file the conversion filled carries a
  `born` dated by the conversion write rather than by the element. Where the derived birth
  is earlier, that placeholder is what is being corrected and the tool drops it, naming it
  in the run's output; where the placeholder's date *is* the birth, no earlier born arrives
  and it stands. The dates decide, so neither truncating these files as a class nor leaving
  them is the rule. Only the conversion's own entry is ever replaced - an entry somebody
  wrote is never dropped, whatever its date.
- **Open a file the marking pass could not.** An element retired *before* that pass is named
  by no carrier, so nothing will ever create its file. A `--backfill` batch that opens with
  `born` creates it; its whole history, birth through `retired`, arrives at once or not at
  all. Do not put such a history on `_pack.md` instead: a `retired` entry seals the file it
  ends, and `_pack.md` is the one file in a pack that must stay appendable forever.

Every other caller - every change being made now - uses the plain lane, where a file only
ever grows at its end.

## 2. The README carries use, never history

A pack's `README.md` is for the person adopting the pack or reaching for one of its
elements: when the pack activates, what each check demands and what satisfies it, when a
skill is the thing to load, what the task does to the repository, and the catalog of what
the pack carries. Never how an element came to be, what it replaced, why its id reads as it
does, what an earlier shape did, or how the pack is maintained. The test is the sentence: a
date, a pull request number, an "until", a "was", a "kept as it was" or a "distilled from"
is a decision, and a decision is an entry on the element's file - `_pack.md` for the pack's
own shape. Move it there; do not write it here.

## 3. The mount is never edited

A file under `.claudinite/shared/` arrived from a canon and the next converge replaces the
whole tree. Change it in the canon, or carry the difference in the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`.

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.
